In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

UVB light, the major carcinogen for nonmelanoma skin cancers, induces CPD preferentially at dipyrimidines, which are located in a specific DNA sequence context and which are frequently found in the p53 gene, the major target for UVB‐related mutagenesis.
CPD hot spots are formed at PyrmC sites, but that this effect is enhanced by methylation at the 5′‐position.
UVB‐inducible CPD are the major mutagens in human nonmalignant skin cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the distribution patterns of CPDs in the human genome and in the p53 gene are not only influenced by the sequence of the DNA but also by the methylation status of the DNA and the chromatin structure.
the UVB mutagenic potential for p53 gene is determined by both the sequence‐specific UVB damage pattern and the sequence‐specific DNA folding pattern.
the p53 hot spots in skin cancer result from a combination of the following three factors: (i) the sequence specificity of UVB light, (ii) DNA folding in nucleosomes, and (iii) DNA methylation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the UVB‐inducible mutational spectrum in p53 is a reflection of the UVB‐mediated DNA damage spectrum and that the mutational hotspots in p53 are a result of UVB‐inducing CPD in DNA.
UVB‐induce CPD frequency in vivo correlates with skin cancer mutational hotspots in p53 and that DNA methylation may play an important role in the formation of CPD.

UVB‐inducible CPD formation is a major factor in the mutagenesis of human skin cancer and that the mutational hot spots in p533 are due to the UVB‐inducing CPD formation at CC and PyrMC positions, as well as the increased CPD formation at PyrmC in methylated DNA.
